result: Grid cells exhibit two distinct firing modes: task-anchored firing (68/103 cells) where activity is anchored to the virtual track reference frame, and task-independent firing (32/103 cells) where periodic activity is decoupled from the task environment and encodes distance traveled independently.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly acknowledge and accept this core finding. The editor states 'the authors demonstrate that grid cells can either fire in relation to the position relative to task-relevant virtual stimuli or independently based on the distance covered,' and Reviewer 3 confirms 'grid cells could fire in at least two modes' with task-anchored and task-independent characteristics. The data classification and periodogram analysis are not questioned.

result: Grid cells can switch between task-anchored and task-independent firing modes within a single behavioral session, with 73.8% of grid cells showing no single coding scheme accounting for more than 85% of trials.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'the anchoring of activity patterns could switch within a behavioral session' as a strength of the study. The within-session variability is treated as a key observation that distinguishes this work from prior studies.

result: Grid cells transition between firing modes coherently as a population, with simultaneously recorded grid cells switching at the same time, consistent with continuous attractor dynamics.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the coherent switching observation. Reviewer 2 states 'the authors found that, interestingly, grid cell activity pattern could be anchored to task reference frame or maintain a periodic pattern independent of the reference frame' and notes the population-level coordination. The interpretation regarding attractor dynamics is not challenged.

result: Non-grid cells in MEC form multiple populations: some switch coherently with grid cells while others maintain stable task-anchored representations independently, with task-independent periodic firing being rare among non-grid cells.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 identifies this as a weakness, noting 'it is unclear whether and how the coding scheme is associated with behavior' for non-grid cells. While the observation of heterogeneity is accepted, reviewers indicate the functional significance and behavioral relevance of these distinct non-grid populations requires further investigation.

result: On cued trials where the reward location is marked by a visual beacon, behavioral performance is similar regardless of whether grid cells are task-anchored or task-independent, suggesting grid representations are not required for cued navigation.
evaluation: The editor states 'their findings convincingly reveal that mice exhibited better performance in the path integration task when grid cell activity was anchored' and Reviewer 3 notes 'when a unique visual cue marked the reward location, navigation performance was not correlated with the grid cells' firing mode.' This dissociation is accepted as a key finding.

result: On non-beaconed and probe trials requiring path integration, task-anchored grid firing is associated with spatially organized stopping behavior and higher success rates compared to task-independent firing.
evaluation: All reviewers affirm this central finding. The editor emphasizes 'mice exhibited better performance in the path integration task when grid cell activity was anchored to their position on the virtual track rather than the distance traversed.' Reviewer 3 states 'on trials in which the rewarded location was unmarked, the behavioral performance of mice was better when grid cells fired in the task-anchored mode.' This correlation is treated as convincing evidence.

result: Task-anchoring of grid cells to the environment selectively enhances performance when path integration is required, supporting hypothesized roles for grid cells in path integration while arguing against a general-purpose spatial coding function.
evaluation: The editor describes the work as 'highlighting the contribution of grid firing to spatial navigation behavior' and Reviewer 3 states 'the link proposed by Clark and Nolan between task-anchored coding by grid cells and navigational performance is a significant step toward better understanding how grid cell activity might support behavioral behavior.' The selective enhancement interpretation is accepted.

result: Switches in grid cell firing mode occur in blocks extending across multiple trials and cannot be explained by variation in cue or reward availability, with block length distribution significantly different from shuffled data.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical question about causality: 'whether the activity anchoring switched first, or the task behaviors altered first, or whether they happened within the same trial' to determine if encoding is causal for behavior. While the block structure is not disputed, the temporal relationship and causal direction remain unclear according to reviewers.

result: 103 out of 1881 neurons were identified as grid cells with field sizes of 7.5±3.3 cm and grid spacing of 72.5±13.7 cm, located in dorsomedial MEC.
evaluation: These basic characterization data are not questioned by any reviewer. The grid cell identification and properties are treated as standard methodological outcomes.

result: Residual localization performance on task-independent trials suggests additional neural mechanisms beyond task-anchored grid firing may support path integration-dependent behavior.
evaluation: This acknowledgment of incomplete dependence on grid anchoring is implicitly accepted by reviewers. Reviewer 3 notes the study is 'correlative' and that 'selective manipulations of grid cell activity on the virtual task will be needed to evaluate whether the activity of grid cells is causally linked,' which aligns with the authors' recognition of alternative mechanisms.

result: The mode switching observed differs from previously reported spontaneous remapping of MEC network states, as it involves switching between task-anchored representations useful for the task and task-independent representations unlikely to contribute to task solution.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this distinction from prior work. The characterization of the switching phenomenon as functionally relevant (between useful and non-useful representations) is accepted without objection.
